title: 2026 09 02 - HE
machineSummary: Jessica Sandoval of Endo Warriors Aotearoa, Cleaver, and Lucy said Health New Zealand’s adaptation of Australian guidelines is insufficient. They called for a funded national endometriosis action plan. Debates focused on systemic diagnosis delays, GP education barriers, and the need for gender-inclusive healthcare.

chunks.text: Being available. I know it was quite short notice when we an invite to do so. It's ultimately great to be here- Thank you for having us... uh, within a week, um, on this very important matter. And, uh, we have you in here for a 10-minute hearing. Uh, I'm Sam McEntyre, chair of the committee. You'll see members around the table with, with name tags.

Um, you've got 10 minutes to, to discuss, um, if you want to leave us time for questions, you may, but I'll leave that up to you. Okay. I'm sure some members would like the opportunity, though. So, um, I'll hand that over, and you can introduce yourself and, and go from there. Thank you. Okay. Um, tena koutou katoa. My name is Jessica Sandoval, and I am the founder of Endo Warriors Aotearoa. For more than 20 years, I have lived in pain with endometriosis. I've experienced nine pregnancy losses- Oh, wow... multiple surgeries that caused lasting damage, a hysterectomy that did not cure

endometriosis, and the loss of my ability to work full time. I know the cost of being dismissed. This petition and our guideline review is not about one voice. Our lived experience booklet records childhood symptoms, missed school, lost jobs, rejected referrals, misleading normal scans, and surgery without follow-up.

And every day, I hear from people still living with the same experience, reaching out for support because they don't know where else to turn. This is not historic failure. They are happening now. Different people, different post codes, the same pattern. Dismissal, delay, inadequate treatment. On the 18th of August, the government announced that Health New Zealand will adapt Rings Australia's living evidence guidelines in Aotearoa.

We welcome that direction, but the 2020 guidelines already support clinical diagnosis in primary care and recognize that a normal examination or ultrasound does not exclude endometriosis. People still wait for answers for years. The failure was never only the wording. It was the implementation, access, accountability, and lack of funding.

But treating... Um, sorry. Training is being developed. Extra pain and anal support is being explored. But explored is not funded. A political announcement is not implementation. A press release is not a care pathway. If a GP diagnoses endometriosis, what happens next?

Can that person access imaging, pain care, specialist care, fertility support, or surgery, or are they simply given a diagnosis and left waiting? Our full review contains many recommendations. These five are not the whole answer. They are the minimum starting point. First, national pathways with timelines.

Persistent sy- sy- symptoms must trigger review and a referral. A declined referral cannot be the end of care. Second, national standards for imaging. A routine pelvic exam, scan is not a specialist endometriosis scan, and negative imaging does not exclude superficial endometriosis.

Specialist endometriosis ultrasound is very limited in Aotearoa. This expertise must not be limited by post code or someone's ability to pay. People in rural and regional communities are already missing out, and specialist imaging cannot become something that's only available for those who can travel and afford to pay for care. Third, genuine treatment choice.

The guidelines being adapted at the moment continue to pos- position hormonal medication as the first line of treatment. Hormonal treatment helps many people, but it does not work for everyone and should not become an automated answer. Symptom suppression is not the same as a cure, and research shows that pain can return just as worse after hormonal treatment.

Endometriosis can also affect fertility, so fertility goals need to be considered early, not just when someone wants to try for pregnancy. People need informed choice, regular reviews, and publicly funded access to pelvic health physios, pain care, ferti- fertility support, and evidence-informed holistic and complementary care. Fourth, youth specific culturally safe and inclusive care. Rangatahi need education and clinicians who recognize the warning signs of endometriosis early. Care must include women, girls, alongside trans, non-binary,

intersex, and gender diverse people. Lived experience must have real decision-making power from the beginning, including Maori, Pacific, rural, disabled, youth, and rainbow voices. Young people need to learn the warning signs of endometriosis early. Endo Warriors Aotearoa is already delivering this education in schools, 300 students so far this year, but access should not depend on whether a small charity can secure enough funding to keep it going.

This needs to be available nationally. Fifth, accountability. Publish the implementation timelines, funding, workforce plan, referral criterias, waiting times, diagnostic delays, and patient outcomes. Measure whether inequities actually shrink, and report the results publicly. We need a funded national endometriosis action plan.

Please not, do not mistake early diagnosis for complete care. Do not move people from waiting for a diagnosis to waiting with a diagnosis. The people in our booklet revealed medical trauma, pregnancy loss, opportunities of jobs, and years of pain so you could understand their stories.

Their evidence is not anecdotal noise. When the same harm repeats across ages, regions, and communities, it is a pattern. And when that system knows that pattern and does not act, delay becomes policy choice. Let the 13-year-old in pain today hear something better than enou- another promise. Nga mihi nui. I'll now pass on to Cleaver.

Thank you. Um, kia ora. My name is Cleaver. For me, endometriosis was never just a painful period. As soon as I started getting periods, something was wrong. Before testosterone and a total hysterectomy, I essentially had a constant period. I was losing huge amounts of blood, in severe pain, dizzy, sick, getting migraines, and struggling with my back and bowels.

I went to the school nurse over and over because there wa- But because there was nothing visibly wrong with me, I wasn't believed. Years later, someone finally said to me, "Your body is not normal. This is not normal." That was the beginning of understanding I might have endometriosis. I am also a gender fluid trans man, and that has added another layer to an already difficult illness.

I have been intentionally misgendered during treatment. I have had medical staff struggle to understand how I could be male and have endometriosis, but those two things can exist together. That misunderstanding has meant barriers to care, dismissal, and having to educate medical professionals about my existence while already in extreme pain.

After more than eight years on testosterone and having a total hysterectomy, some things have improved. Medical cannabis has also given me back parts of my life I had lost to pain. But I can still go to the emergency department and be labeled as drug-seeking instead of receiving the care I need.

Endometriosis is not simply a woman's illness. Trans, gender diverse, and non-binary people can have endometriosis too, and healthcare needs to recognize us. Sometimes the most important thing you can give someone with endometriosis is simple: believe them.

Thank you. Um, and I'm going to pass on to Lucy. Mm. Nga mihi nui. Kia koutou katoa. Ko Lucy toku ingoa. I'm here today not just to share my story with you, but to show you what this illness and Aotearoa's unjust healthcare system is doing to those affected by it. For five years now, I've been thrown a new birth control or pain medication every few months just for it to be a short-term fix or sometimes make everything worse.

Five years of being given temporary solutions for a condition so debilitating. I've been sent from doctor to doctor waiting months and months for an appointment, or up until last week, one and a half years just to see a gynecologist. With a system like this, new symptoms often get ignored, things get missed, information doesn't get passed on.

Every appointment I go to, I walk in hoping that I'm finally moving forward with treatment, only to leave with a new prescription in hand. I'm fatigued from pain medications and getting h- constant headaches because my hormones are so unstable, but no one listens when I say thing, I think things are getting worse. Just because I get up every day, I study, go to work, or do things that bring me joy, it does not mean I'm getting better. It does not mean I am okay.

It means that despite the pain I'm in, nearly every day, I'm not letting this illness control my life any more than it already has. At 20 years old, I should not be living my life like this. No one should spend so long simply waiting for an answer. But for those with endometriosis, this is the reality. Thank you very much. Thank you.

Very touching submissions from all of you. Does anyone have a question they would like to ask? We've got about one minute. Dr. Chung. sure. I just want to get a little bit more detail. When you talk about 20 years old as a young lady, and experience with this, what is the major obstacle or challenges when you go to see your GP?

Is it because they don't believe, or they just don't have the knowledge to identify the issues? Can you give us a little bit more information? I have constantly been told they think it is my anxiety, my ADHD. They just believe it is related to something that I was diagnosed with at a younger age. But because I look healthy, because I don't take pain medication half the time because it gives me so many other side effects, they think it's completely fine, and they think that because I'm so young, I don't have this illness because it's not showing up on any scans, because I haven't tried to get

pregnant and had a miscarriage, anything like that. All right. We have people with you, and I'm sure all of us will have family members or loved ones that have gone through horrific journeys with endometriosis. Dr. Carroll. Thanks for outlining those five points.

They're all good points that our system should be seeking to achieve. You didn't come down on a particular model for what good endometriosis services should be, and I wonder if you're able to comment on that. Dr. Chung has asked about general practice.

I know in Australia they have specialist women's health clinics that are more accessible in the community. Could you expand a little on what you think good care in a responsive health system looks like? I think the biggest obstacles that I hear from people all the time at the moment is getting to the GPs. Enough people don't see the same GP constantly because it's too hard to book in and the costs involved. So that's the first obstacle.

Then the next is the GPs not having all the knowledge, and that's understandable. You don't know everything, and you've always got to learn. So there's always things they have to learn on. And it's not having the knowledge, and then also putting the referrals through. But since COVID, a lot of hospitals aren't accepting gynecology referrals- Yeah... so a lot of people are missing out.

We've had people that have traveled overseas to India and stuff like that for surgeries. So there's the referrals not being accepted. Then there's the hospitals are hugely understaffed. We hear about the wait times in ED and things like that. I was sent to ED earlier this year because I had a cyst that was leaking blood, and it was very painful, so my doctor said I had to go in.

I sat there for 12 hours to be told to go home, take the morphine that I had at home, and to be aware that my next period might be worse. I had mentioned four times I had a hysterectomy. So I don't blame that doctor. The ED was overrun. So a good system would be, I guess, tracking everything from the beginning.

In an ideal world, it would be great if all the medical systems talked to each other. I'm very fortunate to be under the pain specialist team in Wellington and have a great doctor, and he actually physically goes and talks to my neurologist when I was with cardiology and everything. Talks to everyone to put a plan in place. But that's not feasible for everyone.

Thank you. We are past time. I want to thank you all for coming in here and sharing your experiences. Very useful for the committee. And we hear you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you for having us. Thank you. Appreciate it. Thank you.
